## Instructions

For each problem, please write complete arguments, not only calculations. Your 

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">1</span> **Divisibility is transivitive.** Prove directly from the definition of divisibility that if $a\mid b$ and $b\mid c$, then $a\mid c$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">2</span> **Division algorithm.** In this problem, we prove the division algorithm which asserts that for any integers $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $b\ne0$, there exist unique integers $q,r\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that 
$$a=qb+r,\qquad 0<=r<|q|.$$ 

(1) Let $x$ be a real number. Denote by $m and $n$ the greatest integer not exceeding $x$ and the least integer no less than $x$, respectively. Show $x-1<m\le x\le n<x+1$.

(2) Prove the existence part of the division algorithm by taking $q$ to be the greatest integer not exceeding $a/b$ when $b>0$ and the least integer no less than $a/b$ when $b<0$.

(3) Prove the uniqueness part of the division algorithm: If there are $q_1,q_2,r_1,r_2\in\mathbb{Z}$ with such that 
$$\begin{align}
a &= q_1b + r_1,\qquad 0<=r_1<|q_1|,\\
a &= q_2b + r_2, \qquad 0<=r_2<|q_2|,
\end{align}$$
then $q_1=q_2$ and $r_1=r_2$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">3</span> **Definition of ideal.** Show that for any $a,b\in\Z$, the set $I_{a,b}=\{ax+by:x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">4</span> **Multiplying congruences.** Use the definition of congruennce to show that if $a_1\equiv b_1\pmod{m}$ and $a_2\equiv b_2\pmod{m}$, then $a_1a_2\equiv b_1b_2\pmod{m}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">5</span> **Modulo powers of 2.** (1) Show that the square of every odd integer is congruent to $1$ modulo $8$. 

(2) Show by induction that for any odd integer $a$ and any integer $n>=3$, we have $a^{2^{n-2}}\equiv 1\pmod{2^{n}}$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">6</span> **A divisibility test.** Prove that an integer is divisible by $3$ if and only if the sum of its decimal digits is divisible by $3$.

<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Use $10\equiv1\pmod3$ and write the integer in base 10 decimal expansion.
</details>
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">7</span> **Euclidean algorithm.** Compute $\gcd(2026,748)$ and express the gcd as $2026x+748y$ for integers $x,y$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">8</span> **Linear equations.** Determine whether $84x+126y=30$ has an integer solution. If it does, find all integer solutions; if it does not, prove impossibility.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">9</span> **Modular inverse.** Find the least nonnegative inverse of $37$ modulo $101$, and verify the answer by multiplication.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">10</span> **A structural gcd identity.** Prove that for every positive integer $n$,

$$\gcd(n,n+1)=1.$$

Then generalize: determine $\gcd(n,n+k)$ in terms of $n$ and $k$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">11</span> **Exploration before proof.** Compute $\gcd(F_m,F_n)$ for several Fibonacci numbers and formulate a conjecture. Prove one nontrivial special case of your conjecture, clearly indicating which Fibonacci identities you use.
</div>

## Optional challenge

Prove that consecutive Fibonacci numbers are relatively prime using the Euclidean algorithm rather than a closed formula.
